item.title: Venezuela opposition leader Machado returns home after fraught year away
item.description: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by tens of thousands of cheering supporters as she made her way by car to Caracas on Sunday night, after she arrived home following several failed return attempts which have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump's administration.
item.dc:creator: Vivian Sequera, Sarah Kinosian, Keren Torres
item.content:encoded: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by tens of thousands of cheering supporters as she made her way by car to Caracas on Sunday night, after she arrived home following several failed return attempts which have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump's administration. "This country is giving lessons to everyone," she shouted as her convoy entered the capital, leaning out of the sunroof to shake hands and hug raucous supporters Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging deposed leader Nicolas Maduro for the presidency in 2024, has been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election. On Sunday morning, Machado appeared at a church in western Lara state and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted "liberty!" as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said. She then traveled to the capital in a journey that took eight hours because of crowds. By the time she neared Caracas, festooned in rosaries handed to her by followers, the highway was all but blocked by cheering supporters. "For the reunion of every family, for freedom of every political prisoner, for the freedom of Venezuela," she wrote on social media. Machado's return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed directly on her movements, who added Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it. At the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado's return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez. "She's a very nice woman," he said, referring to Machado. "But we're doing really well in Venezuela.” The White House and the State Department did not respond to Reuters questions on the matter. RETURN PREVIOUSLY DELAYED Machado's efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which [USN:L4N3W51LU TEXT:"she sought to cultivate as an ally"] even before it captured Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial. Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it was [USN:L1N44V0SA TEXT:"too soon to consider democratic elections"] in Venezuela. US officials have asked Machado at least once to [USN:L1N42Y0X4 TEXT:"delay her return"], Reuters reported in June, and she has made [USN:L1N45F02O TEXT:"several failed attempts"] to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details of how she returned. Machado traveled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her trip told Reuters. One person briefed on her movements said the flight took place late last week and US security contractors guarded her during the journey. Rodriguez and the country's authorities were warned by the US not to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said. "The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday. "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy." A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado's political movement. The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Machado's return. SUPPORTERS CHEER MACHADO ON ROUTE "Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela," said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto. Zuleima Granadillo, 61, an employee at the Ministry of Education, waited for Machado at a point on the highway in Aragua state, closer to Caracas. "What does Machado’s arrival mean? All paths are opening up for us, the future is opening up, we have a light, and we are going all the way to the end," she said. "This dictatorship is already over with the arrival of our leader." Machado plans to meet victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters. "She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections," he added. International energy firms committed last month to [USN:L1N44U0I0 TEXT:"expanding projects"] in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Machado has said that only a "serious, democratic government" can provide the stability needed by investors. She had been barred by Maduro's government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding. Machado's Vente Venezuela movement [USN:L6N4611CS TEXT:"released an app on Saturday"] to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls. Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado's movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela.

item.title: Machado sorprende con llegada a Venezuela, seguidores celebran su vuelta
item.description: La líder opositora venezolana María Corina Machado se dirigió a miles de sus seguidores en Caracas el domingo por la noche, tras su regreso a Venezuela, donde fue recibida con vítores por multitudes, luego de varios intentos fallidos de retorno que tensaron sus relaciones con la administración del presidente estadounidense Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Vivian Sequera, Sarah Kinosian
item.content:encoded: La líder opositora venezolana María Corina Machado se dirigió a miles de sus seguidores en Caracas el domingo por la noche, tras su regreso a Venezuela, donde fue recibida con vítores por multitudes, luego de varios intentos fallidos de retorno que tensaron sus relaciones con la administración del presidente estadounidense Donald Trump. "El país le está dando una lección a todos", gritó a sus seguidores al entrar su caravana a la capital. Antes de regresar, Machado, ganadora del Premio Nobel de la Paz, había estado fuera del país durante 10 meses y pasó el año anterior escondida. El domingo por la mañana, apareció por primera vez en una iglesia en el estado occidental de Lara, según imágenes compartidas por su equipo de prensa, y fue recibida por transeúntes que cantaron el himno nacional y gritaron "¡libertad!" mientras partía en una camioneta, según un testigo de Reuters. Durante todo el día, viajó hacia Caracas en una caravana de más de 8 horas, y sus seguidores se agolparon a lo largo del camino. Al acercarse a la capital, la carretera estaba prácticamente bloqueada por la multitud que la aclamaba y varios le obsequiaron rosarios. "Por el reencuentro de cada familia, por la Libertad de cada preso político, por la Libertad de Venezuela", dijo su en redes sociales. Su regreso fue coordinado con los gobiernos de Estados Unidos, Panamá y Colombia, según una persona informada directamente sobre los movimientos y planes de Machado, quien agregó que Trump aprobó su regreso y se mantuvo al tanto. Sin embargo, el domingo en la Casa Blanca, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump dijo que no sabía nada sobre el regreso de Machado y sugirió que Estados Unidos continuaría apoyando a la presidenta encargada venezolana Delcy Rodríguez. "Es una mujer muy agradable", dijo Trump, refiriéndose a Machado. "Pero nos va muy bien en Venezuela". La Casa Blanca y el Departamento de Estado no respondieron a las preguntas de Reuters sobre el asunto. EL REGRESO DE MACHADO SE HABÍA RETRASADO A PETICIÓN DE EEUU Los esfuerzos de Machado, de 59 años, por regresar han puesto a prueba su relación con la administración Trump, a la que ha intentado cultivar como aliada desde antes de que derrocara al expresidente Nicolás Maduro en enero. Trump ha expresado repetidamente su apoyo a Rodríguez, exvicepresidenta del depuesto mandatario Nicolás Maduro, y ha elogiado los acuerdos de producción petrolera y otras iniciativas empresariales de compañías estadounidenses en Venezuela. En septiembre, Trump afirmó que era demasiado pronto para considerar elecciones democráticas en Venezuela. Según informó Reuters en junio, funcionarios estadounidenses le pidieron al menos una vez que retrasara su regreso, y ella ha realizado varios intentos fallidos de ingresar al país. Su equipo no reveló detalles sobre cómo regresó. Machado viajó en un avión privado de Panamá a Colombia y cruzó por tierra el domingo a Venezuela, según informaron a Reuters cuatro personas familiarizadas con sus movimientos. La persona informada directamente sobre sus movimientos indicó que el vuelo tuvo lugar a finales de la semana pasada y que estuvo custodiada por agentes de seguridad estadounidenses durante su viaje. Rodríguez y las autoridades del país fueron advertidas por Estados Unidos de no interferir ni poner en peligro su seguridad, añadió la fuente. El secretario de Estado estadounidense, Marco Rubio, declaró el domingo: "Las condiciones que permiten el regreso seguro de la señora. Machado a Venezuela son el resultado directo de las conversaciones de reconciliación respaldadas por Estados Unidos, que ya han propiciado la liberación de cientos de presos políticos y el regreso del exilio de cientos de figuras de la oposición". "Esperamos que todos los actores políticos apoyen estas conversaciones, que representan la mejor oportunidad que Venezuela ha tenido en treinta años para lograr pacíficamente no solo unas elecciones libres y justas, sino también una democracia duradera". Una facción de la oposición y el gobierno encargado mantuvieron una ronda de conversaciones este mes, con el objetivo de reformar el Tribunal Supremo de Justicia y el Consejo Nacional Electoral, entre otros, de cara a las eventuales elecciones. El movimiento político de Machado no ha participado en las conversaciones. El Ministerio de Comunicación de Venezuela, que gestiona todas las consultas de prensa del gobierno, no respondió de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentarios sobre el regreso de Machado. SIMPATIZANTES DAN VIVAS A MACHADO CAMINO A CARACAS Mientras Machado viajaba hacia la capital el domingo, miles de personas se congregaron a los lados de la carretera. Gritando: "María, te amamos", "bienvenida" y "libertad". Machado divulgó fotos y videos de decenas de personas saludándola en la carretera mientras ella avanzaba en una camioneta blanca y se detenía en varios tramos para saludar. En Santa Mónica, una zona del sur de Caracas, Mercedes Márquez, una docente jubilada de 54 años, dijo que “lo que queremos es fecha de elecciones y que María Corina sea la candidata. Queremos cambios y que esta gente que nos ha destruida la vida 25 años se vaya". "No hemos visto, los ciudadanos, ningún cambio desde el 3 de enero. Todo parece igual o peor", agregó Márquez al referirse a la fecha en que Estados Unidos capturó en un operativo militar en Caracas al presidente Nicolás Maduro. El Gobierno de Maduro le prohibió a Machado salir de Venezuela, pero ella partió en secreto a finales de 2025 para recibir el Nobel de la Paz, después de pasar más de un año viviendo en la clandestinidad. Más temprano, el presidente Trump, al ser consultado sobre el regreso de Machado, dijo que "no sé nada al respecto. Pero creo que es una mujer muy agradable. Me entregó su Premio Nobel, así que ¿cómo podría decir otra cosa? Y espero que esté a salvo." En agosto, una facción de la oposición y el Gobierno encargado, bajo el apoyo de Estados Unidos, iniciaron conversaciones en busca de reformar el sistema político del país antes de las elecciones, en un proceso en el que no está participando Vente Venezuela, el movimiento de Machado. Machado planea reunirse con las víctimas de los terremotos que azotaron Venezuela en junio, así como con las familias de los prisioneros políticos, dijo a Reuters David Smolansky, su principal asesor de asuntos exteriores. "Ella trabajará de manera proactiva para fijar una fecha para elecciones libres y justas", añadió. El movimiento opositor de Machado se prepara para unas [USN:L6N4681I5 TEXT:"eventuales elecciones"], lo que incluye una nueva iniciativa para impulsar el registro de votantes, según documentos y fuentes conocedoras del asunto.

item.title: Brazil’s Lula wins historic fourth term, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede
item.description: Senator Bolsonaro led the election's first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes. The shock result defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
item.dc:creator: Lisandra Paraguassu, Brendan O'Boyle, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes
item.content:encoded: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. However, his opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept defeat and said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Sunday ruling from a Supreme Court justice that extended voting for two hours. Bolsonaro led the election's first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets which had bet on his victory. His refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father's reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the Supreme Court to 27-years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power. The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro's loss to Lula — by more than twice his father's losing margin — and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the conservative-leaning south make any annulment unlikely, analysts said. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but "it's very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result." COMEBACK KING [USN:L6N46C031 TEXT:"Investors expect"] recent bets on a change of government to unwind in a volatile week ahead on financial markets. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index (1325.T) dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory, while the Brazilian real was set to fall sharply against the US dollar. The victory marks another comeback in a career full of them for Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. "He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters. At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of [USN:L6N43W1JI TEXT:"corruption scandals"] and [USN:L6N459162 TEXT:"rising prices"], while sweeping social changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its [USN:L1N44902P TEXT:"growing ranks of informal workers"]. Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty. "People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said. During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term. He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"led a campaign"] to get the Bolsonaros back to power. Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration. There was no immediate comment from Trump or the US State Department, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Latin American leaders were quick to[USN:L2N46C02W TEXT:" offer their congratulations."] Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance." LATE-CAMPAIGN BOOST Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round. His campaign this year mixed the kind of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians. These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented. Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress. CHALLENGES AHEAD Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers. That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations. Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow just 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic. Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model. Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign. The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.

item.title: Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
item.description: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
item.dc:creator: Ivana Sekularac, Edward Mcallister, Aleksandar Vasovic
item.content:encoded: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country. Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014. But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of [USN:L8N4650K6 TEXT:"student-led demonstrations"] against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. "It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won," Vucic said in a televised speech. Within moments of his announcement, the streets of [USN:L6N46B0A6 TEXT:"Belgrade erupted in celebration"]. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city's main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting "victory" and "he's done". The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently , against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results. "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future." European leaders and officials [USN:L6N46B0AC TEXT:"congratulated the Student List on its victory,"] among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. "We stand ready to...work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen wrote on X. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country's support. RECORD TURNOUT SPURS STUDENTS TO VICTORY Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. "(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast. Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. "Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vucic said. UNCERTAINTY OVER THE STUDENTS' CANDIDATES Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic's announcement. However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students' domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions. As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner. "The biggest uncertainty is...who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia's position in foreign policy," said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant. PROTEST MOVEMENT INCREASED PRESSURE The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since. Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates. "We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends. Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process.

item.title: Saudis say Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
item.description: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target". King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the militant group continued unabated. The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked. The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran , turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. FLIGHT TRACKING DATA SHOWS LITTLE TRAFFIC After Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would "never be safe" and urged airlines, airport staff and travellers not to use it. Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday. Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11. MISSILE AND DRONE ATTACKS CONTINUE Saudi civil defense said on Sunday that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles. Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed. The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements. Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier.

item.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris
item.description: It was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer that enabled Trump to pursue foreign-policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, [USN:L1N3Q1127 TEXT:"“energy dominance”"] was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections . Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to [USN:S0N3NI004 TEXT:"“unleash American energy”"], prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war , and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the [USN:L6N45E05Y TEXT:"Arctic territory"]. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after [USN:L6N3Y407K TEXT:"Washington removed Venezuelan President"] Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently [USN:L1N3ZM1KL TEXT:"took control"] of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record [USN:L03220220 TEXT:"$145 reached in 2008"], when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent [USN:L6N45R160 TEXT:"shipping prices"] skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while [USN:L1N45211Q TEXT:"diesel"] surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including [USN:L6N44M0V8 TEXT:"easing biofuel blending mandates"] and, most controversially, reaching a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel supply agreement"] with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"diesel export ban"], officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly [USN:L6N3ZY18D TEXT:"many in Asia"], the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing. item.title: Ready for a French test?: Five questions for the ECB
item.description: The European Central Bank meets on Thursday against a backdrop of upheaval in France and an Iran war that is keeping energy prices above $100, meaning inflation risks remain elevated.
item.dc:creator: Dhara Ranasinghe, Stefano Rebaudo
item.content:encoded: The European Central Bank meets on Thursday against a backdrop of [USN:L2N46A01A TEXT:"upheaval in France"] and an Iran war that is keeping energy prices above $100, meaning inflation risks remain elevated. "How do you set rates against that backdrop? It's incredibly difficult," David Coombs, head of multi-asset investments at Rathbones Asset Management, said. Here's a look at five key questions for markets ahead of the October meeting. 1/ What will the ECB do? Leave its key interest rate unchanged at 2.5%. A pause is widely anticipated after the ECB raised rates in June and [USN:L1N452054 TEXT:"September"] to counter rising inflation, as the Iran war pushed up energy prices. Economists polled by Reuters [USN:L6N45T0G5 TEXT:"expect a quarter-point rate hike"] in December. "I don't think they've become materially less worried about inflation here," MUFG senior economist Henry Cook said. 2/ What will the ECB say about the rate outlook? It's likely to stick with a data-dependent approach. Caught between high inflation, at [USN:L8N45O0I3 TEXT:"3.8% in September"], and concerns that [USN:L1N45N082 TEXT:"rising government bond yields"] could hurt growth, policymakers have recently argued for what ECB President Christine Lagarde called a "[USN:L8N45K12P TEXT:"measured response"]." "There will be a definite flag to the tightening in financial conditions and how it should slow growth and hence curb inflationary pressures," said Barclays' head of euro rates strategy Rohan Khanna. "But also, plenty of uncertainty around the conflict and the outlook for energy prices." 3/ How worried is the ECB about an energy-driven inflation rise? Comments from officials such as ECB chief economist [USN:S8N3YE046 TEXT:"Philip Lane suggest"] the ECB is not overly worried, for now, about high energy costs leading to other prices and wages rising. A muted increase in core inflation, which excludes food and fuel prices, to [USN:L8N45O0I3 TEXT:"2.5% last month from 2.4%,"] suggests that high energy costs have yet to generate the sort of second-round impacts that could set off a hard-to-break inflation spiral. Still, with oil up 90% this year and headline inflation above its 2% target, the ECB will likely stress vigilance. Euro zone consumers [USN:L8N41P0P6 TEXT:"nudged up their inflation"] expectations for the next 12 months in September, a survey on Friday showed. "If the war in Iran escalates, or if we see further pressure on energy prices, the risk is still more rate hikes in 2027," said Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist at Rabobank, adding he did not have any penciled in for next year. Markets price in at least two hikes by mid-2027. 4/ What about the French bond selloff? Well, the ECB is watching. French 10-year borrowing costs just hit [USN:L8N4670MT TEXT:"24-year highs above 5%"] and a weakened government is grappling with violent protests that could undermine efforts to improve fragile finances. Also, the premium investors demand to hold 10-year French bonds over safer Germany is at 167 bps, up from 92 bps when the ECB met last month. But don't expect the ECB to act soon with measures such as the [USN:L1N45N0CH TEXT:"Transmission Protection Instrument"] that allows it to buy bonds from any member state experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of its financing conditions. France should [USN:L1N46002V TEXT:"solve its own debt problems"] through fiscal consolidation, says Lagarde. The ECB could hold back on rate hikes if it thinks a crisis in France could hurt economic growth materially, Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding said. "If there are serious contagion effects from a hypothetical French crisis to other countries where the fiscal policy is much more sustainable, the ECB would probably use its TPI to shield these other countries, not France," he said. 5/ Who will replace Lagarde? The ECB chief, who could be appointed as the [USN:L6N4610XU TEXT:"next World Economic Forum chair"] as early as November, will likely be pressed on succession. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, [USN:FWN45G19M TEXT:"Klaas Knot"] and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners. Lagarde's exit would open a second vacancy on the ECB's six-member Executive Board after [USN:L6N45V0R7 TEXT:"Isabel Schnabel's recent resignation"]. Chief economist Lane will step down in May. Lagarde's term is scheduled to end next October. Leaving early allows time for a new ECB chief to be picked before France's spring presidential election. A snap Spanish election could also impact the [USN:L8N46305T TEXT:"politics around ECB succession"], analysts said.

item.content:encoded: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe Les valeurs à suivre lundi à la Bourse de Paris et en Europe : Eurazeo nomme un Christophe Bavière président du directoire 26 octobre (Reuters) - Eurazeo a annoncé lundi la nomination de Christophe Bavière comme président unique du directoire du groupe d'investissement français, dans la perspective de l’échéance des mandats en cours, le 5 février 2027. États-Unis: Le moral des ménages se dégrade moins que prévu en octobre, selon une enquête de l'Université du Michigan Le moral des ménages américains s'est dégradé moins que prévu en octobre, montrent vendredi les résultats définitifs de l'enquête mensuelle de l'Université du Michigan. Moody's maintient la note souveraine de la France à "Aa3" L'agence de notation Moody's a décidé vendredi de maintenir la note de crédit de la France à "Aa3", assortie d'une perspective négative, alors que la plupart des analystes s'attendaient à une dégradation à "A1". Stellantis, Bolt et Grand Paris veulent lancer des services de mobilité autonome dès 2028 Stellantis, l'entreprise estonienne de VTC Bolt et la région Île-de-France prévoient de lancer un programme de conduite autonome dans la capitale française en 2028, en utilisant des véhicules du constructeur franco-italo-américain, ont-elles annoncé vendredi dans un communiqué commun. La Royaume-Uni recommande à la population d'avoir des réserves d'urgence pour trois jours Le gouvernement britannique a conseillé vendredi à la population de disposer chez elle de réserves d'urgence pour trois jours, une recommandation qui, selon lui, a été renforcée par le bug logiciel PHP de cette semaine, ainsi que par un été record marqué par la canicule, la sécheresse et les incendies de forêt. AmEx relève son objectif de bénéfice grâce aux dépenses de sa clientèle aisée American Express (AmEx) a relevé vendredi son objectif de bénéfice pour 2026 après avoir publié de solides résultats au troisième trimestre de son exercice, tirés, une fois de plus, par les dépenses des clients fortunés. L'Oréal grimpe, la croissance au T3 illustre la résilience des cosmétiques L'action L'Oréal était en nette hausse vendredi en milieu de matinée, le géant français des cosmétiques ayant publié la veille une croissance des ventes trimestrielles supérieure aux attentes, soulignant sa résilience dans un contexte de ralentissement du reste du secteur du luxe. Volkswagen-Les salariés menacent de faire grève si les accords ne sont pas respectés Les dirigeants syndicaux allemands ont menacé d'organiser des grèves chez Volkswagen à partir de janvier, si l'entreprise ne revient pas d'ici fin octobre sur sa récente annulation des accords salariaux, marquant ainsi une escalade des conflits sociaux au sein du groupe. Kering chute de 10% après un nouveau recul des ventes de Gucci L'action Kering dévisse de 10% vendredi, au lendemain des résultats trimestriels du géant français du luxe, marqués par une baisse des ventes de Gucci, sa marque phare, dans un contexte de faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins.

L'Arabie saoudite intercepte des missiles et des drones 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Arabie saoudite a intercepté dimanche des drones et des missiles au-dessus de sa capitale Ryad et du sud de son territoire, a dit la coalition emmenée par les Saoudiens contre les Houthis au Yémen. Russie-Trois morts dans des attaques dans la région de Belgorod MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont été tuées et 13 autres blessées dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche par une attaque de drone ukrainienne contre la ville de Belgorod, en Russie, près de la frontière entre les deux pays, ont déclaré les autorités locales.
